questions.explanation:
The error message "Solution checker fails to export solutions with model-driven app components" indicates
   that the Power Apps Checker (which runs Solution Checker) lacks sufficient permissions to access and
   analyze the components of the model-driven app during the solution export process. Solution Checker is an
   automated tool designed to analyze Power Platform solutions and identify potential issues related to
   performance, reliability, and best practices. It functions by exporting a solution package, unpacking it, and
   running a series of checks on the solution's components.

   Specifically, the error message implies an authorization issue. The Power Apps Checker typically runs under a
   system account. The underlying problem is that the system account which Power Apps Checker utilizes for its
   operations is not properly authorized to read the solution.

   Assigning the Environment Maker security role to the Power Apps Checker application user grants the
   necessary privileges for the Checker to successfully export solutions, including those containing model-
   driven app components. Environment Maker rights allow solution exports which are a crucial pre-requisite for
   solution checking.

   Option A, manually exporting the solution, does not address the underlying permissions issue, so Solution
   Checker would still fail. Option C, assigning the System Administrator role to your user ID, is an excessive
   privilege assignment and is not recommended. Solution Checker should execute without the need for
   elevated permissions to end user accounts. Option D, disabling the Power Apps Checker application user,
   would completely prevent Solution Checker from running. Option E, assigning the Environment Maker security
   role to your user ID, only addresses the user's privileges rather than the Power Apps Checker's authorization.

   Therefore, assigning Environment Maker security role to the Power Apps Checker application user is the best
   resolution.

   Relevant links for further research:

   Use solution checker to validate your apps in Power Apps - Power Apps | Microsoft Learn
   Security roles and privileges - Power Platform | Microsoft Learn

such as read, write, and delete access to data.

during Azure AD registration).

Register the application in Azure AD.
Create an application user in Dataverse.
Assign the necessary security roles to the application user.

or Dataverse table).

Create a reusable component within the app. This allows for modular design and makes the counter
accessible in other parts of the app or other apps if needed.
Components enable encapsulation of functionality, which is essential in this scenario.
3.Create an output parameter and set the value of the parameter to the total number of critical issues.
Add an output parameter to the component to expose the total number of critical issues as a value. This
allows other parts of the app (or other apps) to retrieve and use this data.
The output parameter acts as a dynamic property that returns the critical issues count.
4.Create and format a label to display the total number of critical issues.

output parameter of the component.

Connection Setup:

A data connection is required first to retrieve the data (critical issues count) from the engineering issues list.
Without this, the app cannot access the necessary information.

Component Creation:

Creating a component ensures reusability and modularity. This aligns with Power Apps best practices,
enabling you to use the counter in other apps without redundant configuration.

Output Parameter Configuration:

The output parameter exposes the calculated total to the app. This is crucial for dynamic data handling and
ensures the value is updated as the data changes.

Display the Data:

manner.

questions.stem:
Case study -
This is a case study. Case studies are not timed separately. You can use as much exam time as you would like to
complete each case. However, there may be additional case studies and sections on this exam. You must manage
your time to ensure that you are able to complete all questions included on this exam in the time provided.
To answer the questions included in a case study, you will need to reference information that is provided in the
case study. Case studies might contain exhibits and other resources that provide more information about the
scenario that is described in the case study. Each question is independent of the other questions in this case study.
At the end of this case study, a review screen will appear. This screen allows you to review your answers and to
make changes before you move to the next section of the exam. After you begin a new section, you cannot return
to this section.
To start the case study -
To display the first question in this case study, click the Next button. Use the buttons in the left pane to explore
the content of the case study before you answer the questions. Clicking these buttons displays information such
as business requirements, existing environment, and problem statements. If the case study has an All Information
tab, note that the information displayed is identical to the information displayed on the subsequent tabs. When you
are ready to answer a question, click the Question button to return to the question.
Background -
Northwind Traders uses Microsoft Dynamics 365 Sales to manage its sales process. To better understand its
customers, Northwind Traders invests in a team of researchers who gather data from multiple sources. The
company stores the data it collects in a Microsoft Azure SQL Database. The company plans to use the data to
enrich account records and make the sales team more effective.
Current environment -
Environment -
•The company has three Microsoft Power Platform environments with Dynamics 365 Sales installed. The
environments are named development, test, and production.
•Each environment has an application user that can be used for integrations.
•The company must use solutions to perform all customization and configuration deployment.
Data -
•Researchers are responsible for creating account records.
•Researchers have permissions on the Account table to create records, read all records, and update records they
own.
•A synchronous plug-in runs when an account record is created and could reassign the record to a different user.
•Users must access data as themselves to enforce security and audit changes.
•A column named new_dataid is added to the Account table. The column uniquely identifies which data it should
receive.
•Researchers have researched only the top 20 percent of account records.
Web API -
•The company creates an Azure Function to run a RESTful .NET Web API.
•Data can be retrieved by placing a GET request to the URL https://dataservice-
[ENVIRONMENTNAME].azurewebsites.net/enrich/[DATAID].
•[ENVIRONMENTNAME] is the name of the Microsoft Power Platform environment that requests the data.
•[DATAID] is the new_dataid column in the Account table.
•The Web API response will return a 200 response plus data if the DataId is found. Otherwise, a 404 response is
returned.
•Developers plan to create a custom connector from the Web API to make it accessible from Microsoft Power
Platform.
Requirements -
Custom connector -
•The Web API definition used to create the custom connector must be generated based on a low-code technology.
•The URL used by the custom connector must incorporate the current environment name without hardcoding
values.
•Errors generated by the custom connector must not cause downstream processes to fail.
•Text descriptions and field placeholder text that describe the use of the custom connector must appear for non-
developers.
Process -
•All account records must be updated with data from the Web API once automatically.
•Only account records that contain a DataId should be updated by the Web API.

•Researchers must create Power Automate flows to specify data analysis priority.
•The researchers require a process that repurposes a set of identical steps of parameterized Microsoft Dataverse
queries from a Power Automate flow for use in other flows that have different parameters. The researchers want
to avoid recreating the steps manually each time they create a flow to save time and avoid errors.
Issues -
•A tester attempts to connect to the production instance of the Web API with a DataId that should return data. The
tester receives an error stating that the remote name could not be resolved.
•A missing component causes an error to occur when importing the solution that contains the Power Automate
flow to update account records in a test environment.

questions.explanation:
Justification

Azure Functions (C) – Correct choice

Serverless compute that can execute long-running tasks (up to 10 minutes on the Consumption plan, or
unlimited with Premium/App Service plan).
Automatically scales, integrates with Dataverse triggers, and avoids the 5-minute plug-in timeout.
Supports C#, JavaScript, Python, etc., allowing the same complex calculation logic to be reused with minimal
code changes.

Azure Event Hub (A) – Not suitable

Designed for high-throughput event ingestion and streaming, not for executing custom business logic.
Does not provide a runtime environment for calculations; it only transports data.

Azure Data Factory (B) – Not suitable

Primarily an orchestration service for data movement and transformation pipelines (ETL).
While it can run data flows, it is over-engineered for simple plug-in replacement and lacks direct, low-latency
invocation from Dataverse.

Azure Databricks (D) – Not suitable

A managed Spark cluster geared toward big-data analytics and machine-learning workloads.
Introduces heavy infrastructure overhead and longer provisioning times, making it impractical for
near-real-time, short-lived calculations that previously ran in a plug-in.

Conclusion: Azure Functions best replaces the timed-out plug-in by offering a lightweight, scalable, and
near-real-time execution environment that fits the existing calculation logic and avoids the 5-minute timeout
constraint.

questions.explanation:
Justification

Correct option – A. Use the ReactivateEntityKey action

The CreateEntityKey message fails with EntityKeyIndexStatus.Failed when the underlying index cannot be
created because duplicate values already exist in the key columns.
ReactivateEntityKey forces the platform to re-evaluate the key definition, clears the failed status, and allows
the system to enforce the alternate key after any duplicate rows have been resolved (or after a successful
publish).
This is the first step recommended by the Power Apps/ Power Automate documentation: reactivate the key to
reset its state before attempting any further remediation.

Why the other options are not appropriate as the first step

B. Publish customizations – Publishing merely makes pending changes visible to the environment; it does not
resolve a failed key-creation status caused by duplicate data.
C. DeleteEntityKeyRequest – Deleting the key would remove the definition entirely, requiring you to recreate
it later; it does not address the underlying duplicate-value condition that caused the failure.
D. Delete duplicate combination values in Order ID and Order Date – While removing duplicates is necessary
for a successful key creation, it is an operational data-cleanup step, not the initial action the platform expects
when the key’s status is “Failed.” The proper first step is to reactivate the key so the system can re-evaluate
the definition after cleanup.

Conclusion
The immediate remediation for a failed EntityKeyIndexStatus is to invoke the ReactivateEntityKey action,
which resets the key’s state and prepares the system for subsequent validation or publication. This aligns with
the platform’s prescribed workflow for handling alternate key creation errors.

Justification

The requirement is to automatically generate a default Contact record each time an Account is created.
The standard, supported way to achieve this in Dataverse is to attach a plug-in (or business rule) to the Create
message of the Account entity and, within that plug-in, call IOrganizationService.Create to insert the
Contact. This guarantees the logic runs on every account creation, regardless of how the record is added (UI,
SDK, integration).
Describing a “custom API bound to the account table” introduces an unnecessary abstraction layer. Custom
APIs are intended for external callers, not for internal event-driven logic, and they do not automatically fire on
the entity’s Create message. Adding an API therefore adds configuration overhead and does not ensure the
contact is created reliably.
While using the Organization service inside a plug-in is technically correct, the solution as phrased does not
meet the goal because it does not specify that the plug-in is triggered on the Create message; it merely
mentions a “custom API bound to the account table,” which is not a valid pattern for this scenario.
Consequently, the proposed approach does not satisfy the requirement, making the correct answer B – No.

questions.explanation:
Technical justification

The form’s OnLoad script currently uses Xrm.WebApi.retrieveRecord without any configuration to limit the
payload or to run asynchronously.
Enabling the Async OnLoad app setting tells the platform to execute the OnLoad script in an asynchronous
context, allowing the UI to render first and then fetch the account record in the background. This eliminates
the blocking call that is causing the perceived slowness.
The asynchronous pattern also lets you place the visibility-change logic in the success callback, ensuring it
runs only after the data is actually retrieved, but the key performance gain comes from the async execution
mode itself.
Why the other options are inferior

A – Synchronous XMLHttpRequest – Would block the UI thread, making the form appear even slower and
violating best-practice performance guidelines.
B – Add the code to the success callback – While this is a good practice, it does not address the root cause
(synchronous execution) and therefore does not improve load time on its own.
D – Return only the required column – Reducing the attribute list can shave a few milliseconds, but the
dominant delay is the synchronous call; without async execution the UI still waits for the round-trip.
E – Store the returned data in a global variable – Caching data does not reduce the initial network latency; it
only helps subsequent calls, not the first load.

Conclusion – Enabling the Async OnLoad app setting is the most direct way to improve performance because
it removes the blocking nature of the OnLoad script, allowing the UI to become interactive sooner while the
record is fetched in the background.

References

Model-driven apps – Form scripts and events (Async execution)
Xrm.WebApi.retrieveRecord – Retrieve only needed attributes

Background
Northwind Traders uses Microsoft Dynamics 365 Sales to manage its sales process. To better understand its
customers, Northwind Traders invests in a team of researchers who gather data from multiple sources. The
company stores the data it collects in a Microsoft Azure SQL Database. The company plans to use the data to
enrich account records and make the sales team more effective.
Current environment
Environment

•The company has three Microsoft Power Platform environments with Dynamics 365 Sales installed. The
environments are named development, test, and production.
•Each environment has an application user that can be used for integrations.
•The company must use solutions to perform all customization and configuration deployment.
Data
•Researchers are responsible for creating account records.
•Researchers have permissions on the Account table to create records, read all records, and update records they
own.
•A synchronous plug-in runs when an account record is created and could reassign the record to a different user.
•Users must access data as themselves to enforce security and audit changes.
•A column named new_dataid is added to the Account table. The column uniquely identifies which data it should
receive.
•Researchers have researched only the top 20 percent of account records.
Web API
•The company creates an Azure Function to run a RESTful .NET Web API.
•Data can be retrieved by placing a GET request to the URL https://dataservice-
[ENVIRONMENTNAME].azurewebsites.net/enrich/[DATAID].
•[ENVIRONMENTNAME] is the name of the Microsoft Power Platform environment that requests the data.
•[DATAID] is the new_dataid column in the Account table.
•The Web API response will return a 200 response plus data if the DataId is found. Otherwise, a 404 response is
returned.
•Developers plan to create a custom connector from the Web API to make it accessible from Microsoft Power
Platform.
Requirements
Custom connector
•The Web API definition used to create the custom connector must be generated based on a low-code technology.
•The URL used by the custom connector must incorporate the current environment name without hardcoding
values.
•Errors generated by the custom connector must not cause downstream processes to fail.
•Text descriptions and field placeholder text that describe the use of the custom connector must appear for non-
developers.
Process
•All account records must be updated with data from the Web API once automatically.
•Only account records that contain a DataId should be updated by the Web API.
•Researchers must create Power Automate flows to specify data analysis priority.
•The researchers require a process that repurposes a set of identical steps of parameterized Microsoft Dataverse
queries from a Power Automate flow for use in other flows that have different parameters. The researchers want
to avoid recreating the steps manually each time they create a flow to save time and avoid errors.
Issues
•A tester attempts to connect to the production instance of the Web API with a DataId that should return data. The
tester receives an error stating that the remote name could not be resolved.
•A missing component causes an error to occur when importing the solution that contains the Power Automate
flow to update account records in a test environment.
You need to configure a Dataverse trigger and action in a Power Automate flow so researchers can update account
records with data from the Web API even if they do not have edit privileges on the record.
What should you configure for each trigger and action requirement? To answer, select the appropriate options in
the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

Background
City Power & Light is an energy and utilities company that has offices in Europe. The company subsidizes home
improvements for domestic customers, to improve energy efficiency and to meet environmental commitments. The
company also distributes and generates electricity for domestic and commercial customers. The company has
2,000 employees in multiple offices and in work-from-home locations.
City Power & Light uses a team of schedulers, assessors, field engineers, and customer support agents for home
improvements in a program named Get Energy Fit.
Current Environment
Get Energy Fit Program
City Power & Light uses the following to manage the Get Energy Fit program:
•The company uses a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet named Planning Hub on Microsoft SharePoint Online to store
information about customer appointments, customer details, and customer eligibility in the program.
•The company records sensitive customer information that includes the document identification numbers and the
customer's financial information.
•The company uses an assessor to verify customer eligibility in the program and to perform a suitability
assessment. The assessor completes the suitability assessment by using a paper and clipboard at the customer
property and enters the data to the Planning Hub after the assessment is completed. The assessor also uploads
photographs to an on-premises document library. The assessor completes the eligibility assessment by using an
application written in React.
•Schedulers use Microsoft Outlook to schedule engineers and assessors for home improvement appointments.
About 200 appointments are scheduled daily.
•Employees for the company submit funding claims on behalf of the customer by uploading evidence and
compliance checks information to an application named the Claim Submission Portal.
Technical Environment
•Schedulers use Windows 11 desktop and laptop computers with the latest version of Microsoft Edge.
•Assessors use iOS and Android tablet devices.
•The Claim Submission Portal uses REST-based APIs for all operations and a dedicated testing environment.
Authentication to the API is provided by using the following example header key and value pair:
oAuthentication: 2C8D41431415E429C7FC7A74D8315

•The company uses Microsoft Azure for hosting multiple applications.

Overview

delivery for the Get Energy Fit program.
Business Requirements
•Only team leaders and senior managers should have access to read personally identifiable information (PII).
•All development changes must be tested in a separate environment.
•The company requires out-of-the-box solutions, when possible.
•Sensitive credentials, such as user passwords and API secrets, must be stored securely.
•The Claim Submission Portal must allow citizen developers to create automated solutions.
•Customer and appointment information must be accessible to all applications.
Planning Hub Application
The company is planning to replace the Planning Hub spreadsheet with a new application. The new application has
the following requirements:
•The application must support a component design that provides rapid changes requested by the schedulers.
•The data model for the application must capture the following information:
oInformation about customers such as name, address, and other PII.
oThe data and time for an assessor's or engineer's appointment. Schedulers must be able to view all appointments
without filters.
oRecords the details of the home improvements installed for the customer.
oContains all the information and evidence for submission to the Claim Submission Portal.
•After an assessor uploads the funding application and all evidence after a home improvement has been complete,
the company requires that the status of the application is set to Submit and should run the following:
oRetrieve the details about the customer and the improvement installed.
oSend an approval to a senior manager to review and approve in Microsoft Teams.
oUpload the information to the API endpoint.
oIf the upload fails to complete, it should retry after a delay of 30 seconds up to three times. If an error occurs
after three times, the application should send an email notification to the application support team.
oMust record the status on the funding application.
Suitability Assessment Tool
The company plans to implement a new application named the Suitability Assessment Tool for the assessors. The
new application has the following requirements:
•Must integrate with Microsoft Power Platform.
•Assessors must be able to complete the eligibility assessment by using the Suitability Assessment Tool. The
assessors must be able to upload photographs to the on-premises file share.
•Must be developed by using modular components that can be used by other applications.
•Must be optimized for use on tablet devices.
•All changes to the application must be completed in the Suitability Assessment Tool solution.
Reporting

•The data source for the reporting solution must support incremental refreshes.
•The solution must report accurate data if an error occurs.

questions.explanation:
The solution meets the goal. Here's why:

   The scenario requires passing data from one form (Account) to another (Contact) when opening the Contact
   form using JavaScript. The Xrm.Navigation.openForm function in Power Apps is specifically designed for this
   purpose. This function enables passing parameters to the target form.

   To receive the data parameter passed via Xrm.Navigation.openForm, the target form (Contact form) needs to
   be configured to handle this incoming data. Adding an event handler to the Contact form's OnLoad event is
   the correct approach. Within this event handler, you can access the passed data and use it to modify the
   form's behavior, such as showing or hiding specific sections based on the contact type. This aligns precisely
   with the requirement of adapting the form layout based on the contact type. The data parameter is how you
   will receive the contact type from the initial form.

   By adding the event handler to the "data" parameter in the Contact form editor, you're effectively enabling
   the form to receive and process the contact type information passed from the Account form. This ensures that
   the appropriate form sections are displayed based on the provided data.

   Therefore, adding an event handler for the data parameter is the necessary step to receive and process data
   passed using Xrm.Navigation.openForm, making the solution correct.

   Relevant links for further research:

   Xrm.Navigation.openForm
   Form Event Handlers in Power Apps

Case study -
This is a case study. Case studies are not timed separately. You can use as much exam time as you would like to
complete each case. However, there may be additional case studies and sections on this exam. You must manage
your time to ensure that you are able to complete all questions included on this exam in the time provided.
To answer the questions included in a case study, you will need to reference information that is provided in the
case study. Case studies might contain exhibits and other resources that provide more information about the
scenario that is described in the case study. Each question is independent of the other questions in this case study.
At the end of this case study, a review screen will appear. This screen allows you to review your answers and to
make changes before you move to the next section of the exam. After you begin a new section, you cannot return
to this section.
To start the case study -
To display the first question in this case study, click the Next button. Use the buttons in the left pane to explore
the content of the case study before you answer the questions. Clicking these buttons displays information such
as business requirements, existing environment, and problem statements. If the case study has an All Information
tab, note that the information displayed is identical to the information displayed on the subsequent tabs. When you
are ready to answer a question, click the Question button to return to the question.
Background -
Northwind Traders uses Microsoft Dynamics 365 Sales to manage its sales process. To better understand its
customers, Northwind Traders invests in a team of researchers who gather data from multiple sources. The
company stores the data it collects in a Microsoft Azure SQL Database. The company plans to use the data to
enrich account records and make the sales team more effective.
Current environment -
Environment -
•The company has three Microsoft Power Platform environments with Dynamics 365 Sales installed. The
environments are named development, test, and production.
•Each environment has an application user that can be used for integrations.
•The company must use solutions to perform all customization and configuration deployment.
Data -
•Researchers are responsible for creating account records.
•Researchers have permissions on the Account table to create records, read all records, and update records they
own.
•A synchronous plug-in runs when an account record is created and could reassign the record to a different user.
•Users must access data as themselves to enforce security and audit changes.
•A column named new_dataid is added to the Account table. The column uniquely identifies which data it should
receive.
•Researchers have researched only the top 20 percent of account records.
Web API -
•The company creates an Azure Function to run a RESTful .NET Web API.
•Data can be retrieved by placing a GET request to the URL https://dataservice-
[ENVIRONMENTNAME].azurewebsites.net/enrich/[DATAID].
•[ENVIRONMENTNAME] is the name of the Microsoft Power Platform environment that requests the data.
•[DATAID] is the new_dataid column in the Account table.
•The Web API response will return a 200 response plus data if the DataId is found. Otherwise, a 404 response is
returned.
•Developers plan to create a custom connector from the Web API to make it accessible from Microsoft Power
Platform.
Requirements -
Custom connector -
•The Web API definition used to create the custom connector must be generated based on a low-code technology.
•The URL used by the custom connector must incorporate the current environment name without hardcoding
values.
•Errors generated by the custom connector must not cause downstream processes to fail.
•Text descriptions and field placeholder text that describe the use of the custom connector must appear for non-
developers.
Process -
•All account records must be updated with data from the Web API once automatically.
•Only account records that contain a DataId should be updated by the Web API.
•Researchers must create Power Automate flows to specify data analysis priority.
•The researchers require a process that repurposes a set of identical steps of parameterized Microsoft Dataverse
queries from a Power Automate flow for use in other flows that have different parameters. The researchers want
to avoid recreating the steps manually each time they create a flow to save time and avoid errors.

Issues -
•A tester attempts to connect to the production instance of the Web API with a DataId that should return data. The
tester receives an error stating that the remote name could not be resolved.
•A missing component causes an error to occur when importing the solution that contains the Power Automate
flow to update account records in a test environment.
You need to configure the row filter on the Dataverse trigger.
Which filter should you use?

questions.stem:
Case study -
This is a case study. Case studies are not timed separately. You can use as much exam time as you would like to
complete each case. However, there may be additional case studies and sections on this exam. You must manage
your time to ensure that you are able to complete all questions included on this exam in the time provided.
To answer the questions included in a case study, you will need to reference information that is provided in the
case study. Case studies might contain exhibits and other resources that provide more information about the
scenario that is described in the case study. Each question is independent of the other questions in this case study.
At the end of this case study, a review screen will appear. This screen allows you to review your answers and to
make changes before you move to the next section of the exam. After you begin a new section, you cannot return
to this section.
To start the case study -
To display the first question in this case study, click the Next button. Use the buttons in the left pane to explore
the content of the case study before you answer the questions. Clicking these buttons displays information such
as business requirements, existing environment, and problem statements. If the case study has an All Information
tab, note that the information displayed is identical to the information displayed on the subsequent tabs. When you
are ready to answer a question, click the Question button to return to the question.
Background -
Northwind Traders uses Microsoft Dynamics 365 Sales to manage its sales process. To better understand its
customers, Northwind Traders invests in a team of researchers who gather data from multiple sources. The
company stores the data it collects in a Microsoft Azure SQL Database. The company plans to use the data to
enrich account records and make the sales team more effective.
Current environment -
Environment -
•The company has three Microsoft Power Platform environments with Dynamics 365 Sales installed. The
environments are named development, test, and production.
•Each environment has an application user that can be used for integrations.
•The company must use solutions to perform all customization and configuration deployment.
Data -
•Researchers are responsible for creating account records.
•Researchers have permissions on the Account table to create records, read all records, and update records they
own.
•A synchronous plug-in runs when an account record is created and could reassign the record to a different user.
•Users must access data as themselves to enforce security and audit changes.
•A column named new_dataid is added to the Account table. The column uniquely identifies which data it should

receive.
•Researchers have researched only the top 20 percent of account records.
Web API -
•The company creates an Azure Function to run a RESTful .NET Web API.
•Data can be retrieved by placing a GET request to the URL https://dataservice-
[ENVIRONMENTNAME].azurewebsites.net/enrich/[DATAID].
•[ENVIRONMENTNAME] is the name of the Microsoft Power Platform environment that requests the data.
•[DATAID] is the new_dataid column in the Account table.
•The Web API response will return a 200 response plus data if the DataId is found. Otherwise, a 404 response is
returned.
•Developers plan to create a custom connector from the Web API to make it accessible from Microsoft Power
Platform.
Requirements -
Custom connector -
•The Web API definition used to create the custom connector must be generated based on a low-code technology.
•The URL used by the custom connector must incorporate the current environment name without hardcoding
values.
•Errors generated by the custom connector must not cause downstream processes to fail.
•Text descriptions and field placeholder text that describe the use of the custom connector must appear for non-
developers.
Process -
•All account records must be updated with data from the Web API once automatically.
•Only account records that contain a DataId should be updated by the Web API.
•Researchers must create Power Automate flows to specify data analysis priority.
•The researchers require a process that repurposes a set of identical steps of parameterized Microsoft Dataverse
queries from a Power Automate flow for use in other flows that have different parameters. The researchers want
to avoid recreating the steps manually each time they create a flow to save time and avoid errors.
Issues -
•A tester attempts to connect to the production instance of the Web API with a DataId that should return data. The
tester receives an error stating that the remote name could not be resolved.
•A missing component causes an error to occur when importing the solution that contains the Power Automate
flow to update account records in a test environment.
You need to implement visual hints in the custom connector.
What should you do? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

Get the execution context. The function is passed an execution context as a parameter. This context is an
object that contains all the information about the event that triggered the function (e.g., a field changing, a
form loading). You need this context to access the next level of information.

Use getEventArgs() to get the column name. Within the execution context, the getEventArgs() method
retrieves an object that provides details about the specific event. For a field change event, this object includes
the getEventSource() method, which gives you the control that triggered the event, from which you can get
the column name.

Format and update the correct column. Once you have the column name and the necessary context, you can
use the client-side APIs to format the data or update the column value. This is the final step in the process, as
you must gather all the necessary information before attempting to modify the form.

Correct option: B – Add the URL parameter &ribbondebug=true.

Why it’s the best first step

Enabling ribbon debugging injects additional telemetry and error-reporting into the form’s client-side script
execution.
It surfaces JavaScript console messages, script load failures, and performance bottlenecks that are otherwise

hidden, allowing you to pinpoint the exact cause of the “unresponsive” behavior.
This approach is non-intrusive; you can reproduce the issue with the debug flag on and gather actionable
diagnostics before making any code changes.

Why the other options are less appropriate at this stage

A. Use a Quick View form – Quick Views are meant for lightweight data display, not for diagnosing script
responsiveness; they do not provide any debugging insight.
C. Remove unused forms from the app – While reducing form count can improve overall app performance, it
does not help isolate the specific script-related problem on the affected form.
D. Enable Offline mode – Offline mode changes data caching behavior and is unrelated to client-side script
execution speed or responsiveness.
E. Disable form event handlers – Disabling handlers may mask the symptom but does not reveal why the
scripts are unresponsive; it also risks losing critical functionality needed for diagnosis.

Bottom line: Activating ribbon debugging (&ribbondebug=true) is the precise, low-impact technique to surface
script errors and performance metrics, giving you the information needed to proceed with targeted
optimizations.

questions.explanation:
If-None-Match: null

In Dataverse, an HTTP PATCH request behaves as an upsert operation by default. It will automatically update
the record if it already exists or create it if it doesn't. Setting If-None-Match: null ensures that no conditional
restrictions are placed on the request, allowing both inserts and updates to occur smoothly.

If-None-Match:

To restrict an upsert operation so that it only creates new records and never overwrites existing data, you
must apply the If-None-Match: * header. If Dataverse detects that a record with the specified ID or alternate
key already exists, the precondition fails, and it blocks the update by throwing an HTTP 412 Precondition
Failed error.

Box 1: Security roles -
A security role defines how different users, such as salespeople, access different types of records. To control
access to data, you can modify existing security roles, create new security roles, or change which security
roles are assigned to each user. Each user can have multiple security roles.
Security role privileges are cumulative: having more than one security role gives a user every privilege
available in every role.
Each security role consists of record-level privileges and task-based privileges.

Box 2: OAuth -
Oauth 2.0 is the most frequently used type, which uses the Oauth 2 authentication framework to authenticate
with the service. Before using this authentication type, you'll need to register your application with the service
so that it can receive access tokens for the users.
For example, Register the application in Azure AD shows how to register an application with the Azure Active
Directory service.
During the connection creation process, the user will be asked to enter the credentials for login to the service.
These credentials will be used by the application to get an authorization token. For every request, this
authorization token will be sent to your service through the Authorization header.

Box 3: Basic Authentication -
Basic Authentication is the simplest type of authentication, where the user just has to provide the username
and password to create the connection.
Note: Before using any connector in Azure Logic Apps, Microsoft Power Automate, or Microsoft Power Apps,
the user needs to create a connection by authenticating to the backend service.

Box 3: Global choice -
A choice column provides a list of values for users to pick from. They help streamline data entry in turn
ensuring clean data. There are two types - local and global.

questions.stem:
Case study
This is a case study. Case studies are not timed separately. You can use as much exam time as you would like to
complete each case. However, there may be additional case studies and sections on this exam. You must manage
your time to ensure that you are able to complete all questions included on this exam in the time provided.
To answer the questions included in a case study, you will need to reference information that is provided in the
case study. Case studies might contain exhibits and other resources that provide more information about the
scenario that is described in the case study. Each question is independent of the other questions in this case study.
At the end of this case study, a review screen will appear. This screen allows you to review your answers and to
make changes before you move to the next section of the exam. After you begin a new section, you cannot return
to this section.
To start the case study
To display the first question in this case study, click the Next button. Use the buttons in the left pane to explore
the content of the case study before you answer the questions. Clicking these buttons displays information such
as business requirements, existing environment, and problem statements. If the case study has an All Information
tab, note that the information displayed is identical to the information displayed on the subsequent tabs. When you
are ready to answer a question, click the Question button to return to the question.
Background
Northwind Traders uses Microsoft Dynamics 365 Sales to manage its sales process. To better understand its
customers, Northwind Traders invests in a team of researchers who gather data from multiple sources. The
company stores the data it collects in a Microsoft Azure SQL Database. The company plans to use the data to
enrich account records and make the sales team more effective.
Current environment

Environment
•The company has three Microsoft Power Platform environments with Dynamics 365 Sales installed. The
environments are named development, test, and production.
•Each environment has an application user that can be used for integrations.
•The company must use solutions to perform all customization and configuration deployment.
Data
•Researchers are responsible for creating account records.
•Researchers have permissions on the Account table to create records, read all records, and update records they
own.
•A synchronous plug-in runs when an account record is created and could reassign the record to a different user.
•Users must access data as themselves to enforce security and audit changes.
•A column named new_dataid is added to the Account table. The column uniquely identifies which data it should
receive.
•Researchers have researched only the top 20 percent of account records.
Web API
•The company creates an Azure Function to run a RESTful .NET Web API.
•Data can be retrieved by placing a GET request to the URL https://dataservice-
[ENVIRONMENTNAME].azurewebsites.net/enrich/[DATAID].
•[ENVIRONMENTNAME] is the name of the Microsoft Power Platform environment that requests the data.
•[DATAID] is the new_dataid column in the Account table.
•The Web API response will return a 200 response plus data if the DataId is found. Otherwise, a 404 response is
returned.
•Developers plan to create a custom connector from the Web API to make it accessible from Microsoft Power
Platform.
Requirements
Custom connector
•The Web API definition used to create the custom connector must be generated based on a low-code technology.
•The URL used by the custom connector must incorporate the current environment name without hardcoding
values.
•Errors generated by the custom connector must not cause downstream processes to fail.
•Text descriptions and field placeholder text that describe the use of the custom connector must appear for non-
developers.
Process
•All account records must be updated with data from the Web API once automatically.
•Only account records that contain a DataId should be updated by the Web API.
•Researchers must create Power Automate flows to specify data analysis priority.
•The researchers require a process that repurposes a set of identical steps of parameterized Microsoft Dataverse
queries from a Power Automate flow for use in other flows that have different parameters. The researchers want
to avoid recreating the steps manually each time they create a flow to save time and avoid errors.
Issues
•A tester attempts to connect to the production instance of the Web API with a DataId that should return data. The
tester receives an error stating that the remote name could not be resolved.
•A missing component causes an error to occur when importing the solution that contains the Power Automate
flow to update account records in a test environment.

questions.explanation:
A is correct because registering the plug-in to run synchronously ensures that all operations complete before
returning control to the caller, thus preventing timeouts during external service calls.

Reasoning:

When a plug-in is registered to execute synchronously, it runs in the same thread context as the operation
triggering it, allowing for real-time processing of the tasks, including making multiple web service calls. This

is crucial for ensuring that the required actions are completed sequentially and that no premature termination
occurs due to timeouts associated with asynchronous processing. Real-time interaction with web services
necessitates robust error handling to manage responses effectively, improving the reliability of the
application.

Evaluation of Other Options:

B. Set the HTTP connection KeepAlive property to false: Setting KeepAlive to false may optimize certain
requests, but it does not directly influence the handling of multiple requests or mitigate timeouts. In scenarios
of slow response from the service, this setting could lead to increased latency due to the overhead of
establishing new connections for each request.

C. Register the plug-in by using isolation mode = none: Using isolation mode level "none" allows the plug-in
to run in the same process as the calling assembly but may expose it to more risks and potential failure points.
This mode can lead to issues if the external service fails, impacting the stability of the main process and
increasing the likelihood of timeouts, rather than addressing the core issue of handling external calls
effectively.

D. Assign the IOrganizationService object to a member variable: While this may help optimize service calls
by reusing the service instance, it doesn’t specifically address the timeout scenario or the handling of slow
external requests. The plug-in would still ultimately fail if the external service is unresponsive, regardless of
how the service object is managed.

questions.explanation:
C is correct because setting the HTTP connection timeout value explicitly allows for better control over the
duration of external web service requests, thereby preventing timeouts during slow responses.

In the context of plug-ins in the Microsoft Power Platform, managing external web service calls is critical for
ensuring smooth operational flows. By configuring the HTTP connection timeout, a developer can specify how
long the system should wait for a response before it considers the connection failed. This is particularly
beneficial when external services are unreliable or slow, as it allows the application to remain responsive
rather than timing out abruptly, which can lead to incomplete operations.

Critical Evaluation of Incorrect Options:

A. Register the plug-in to run synchronously. This approach would lead to a synchronous operation that
blocks the execution thread until the service responds. If the external service is slow or unresponsive, this can
cause significant delays or timeouts in the overall process, defeating the purpose of robustness against slow
responses.

B. Register the plug-in by using isolation mode = none. Isolation mode = none runs the plug-in in the same
process as the calling code, which can cause stability issues. If the external web service hangs or crashes, it
could also crash the entire application, making it unsuitable for handling unreliable services.

D. Register the plug-in step once for each web service request. This approach would unnecessarily
complicate the registration process and increase maintenance overhead. It does not enhance the robustness
of handling slow responses, as each registered instance would still suffer from the same timeout limitations
as a single request.

By opting for option C, a developer ensures that the plug-in maintains high responsiveness and resilience
against external service latencies, facilitating overall application stability and user experience.

questions.explanation:
The correct trigger for the cloud flow is C. Dataverse - When a row is added.

Here's why: The canvas app creates rows in a Dataverse table. The core requirement is that when a new row is
created, additional business logic must be executed on a related row. The "Dataverse - When a row is added"
trigger is specifically designed to fire automatically whenever a new row is inserted into the specified
Dataverse table. This aligns directly with the scenario's need to react to row creation events.

Option A, "Dataverse - When an action is performed," requires a specific action to be called which isn't the
intent here, as the trigger should simply react to row creation.

Option B, "Manually trigger a flow," requires manual initiation, contradicting the automatic execution
requirement following row creation in the canvas app. This option would not provide the automatic response

that is necessary for this scenario.

Option D, "Power Apps (V2)," is suitable when the cloud flow needs to be initiated from within the Power App
and passed information from the app. While the app is involved in the broader process, it is the row creation
event in Dataverse that should trigger the business logic, not the Power App directly. The Power Apps (V2)
trigger is designed primarily to accept input from the Power App, which is not required in this scenario - we
only want to respond to the new row creation.

Therefore, the "Dataverse - When a row is added" trigger is the most appropriate choice because it directly
addresses the scenario's need for automated execution of business logic based on the creation of a new row
in a Dataverse table. It's an event-driven approach that simplifies the workflow and ensures that the logic
executes immediately after a new row is added without requiring manual intervention or action calls.

For further reading on Power Automate triggers, particularly those involving Dataverse, refer to these
resources:

questions.explanation:
Technical justification (exam-style)

Option A – Configure the Send Email step to run when the previous step fails
Sets the Run-after condition to “has failed”. This explicitly tells the flow to execute the email action only
when the preceding HTTP activity throws an error, which is exactly the requirement (notify on connection
failure).

Option C – Add a Send Email step after the HTTP step
Places the email action in the flow sequence immediately downstream of the HTTP call. Because the email
step follows the HTTP step, it can be triggered by the failure condition defined inA  . The order is important: the
email must be evaluated after the HTTP action so that its execution context reflects the success/failure of
that call.

Why the other options are unsuitable

B – Add a Send Email step after the Update Dataverse record step – This would cause the email to fire only
when the record-update step fails, not when the HTTP call fails. The failure point is mis-aligned with the

requirement.
D – Update the HTTP step settings and set the retry policy to: None – Changing the retry policy does not
provide any notification mechanism; it merely controls how retries are attempted. It does not trigger an email
on failure.

Conclusion – The combination of A (defining the failure-triggered run-after condition) and C (positioning the
email action right after the HTTP step) correctly implements the needed error-notification logic in the Power
Automate flow.

Why option A is correct

The plug-in must execute under an account that actually possesses the Create privilege on the custom table.
By initializing IOrganizationService with the GUID of a user (or a service account) that already has that
permission, the plug-in runs with the minimum set of rights required – only that user can create rows, and the
plug-in inherits those rights.
This satisfies the principle of least privilege: the plug-in does not grant every user full access; instead it relies
on a dedicated privileged identity to perform the privileged operation on behalf of the caller.

Why the other options are unsuitable

B – Environment Maker role – This role is intended for environment-level customizations, not for granting
table-level write permissions. Granting it to all users would give them broad admin capabilities, violating
least-privilege and creating security over-reach.

C – Run in the User’s Context (Calling User) – When a plug-in runs in the calling user’s context, it inherits that
user’s security rights. Since most users lack the Create privilege on the custom table, the plug-in would fail
for them; the approach does not provide the needed privilege.

D – “Act on Behalf Of Another User” permission – This permission is used for impersonation scenarios (e.g.,
when a user explicitly chooses to act on behalf of another). It does not automatically grant the ability to
create rows, nor does it ensure the plug-in runs with the required rights for all callers.

Implementation tip

using Microsoft.Xrm.Sdk;var service = new OrganizationService(Guid.Parse("UserIdWithCreatePermission"));Entity newRecor

By passing the GUID of a user (or a dedicated service account) that holds the Create right on the custom

table, the plug-in can create rows for any caller while still adhering to least-privilege principles.

questions.explanation:
WhyB  a  nd C are the correct choices

   B – Enable the Async OnSave app setting

   When this setting is turned on, the OnSave event runs asynchronously, giving the platform enough time to
   complete the Xrm.WebApi.updateRecord call without aborting the form save.
   Asynchronous execution prevents the “record not saved” race condition that occurs when the update is forced
   synchronously during the save transaction.

   C – Wrap the update in a promise

   Returning a promise from the OnSave handler tells the framework that the operation is asynchronous and that
   the save should wait until the promise resolves.
   This guarantees that the related record is successfully updated before the current record’s save completes,
   ensuring consistent state across both records.

   Why the other options are not appropriate

   A – Add logic to fire only when the value has changed

   While this reduces unnecessary calls, it does not address the underlying timing issue that causes the related
   record to be missed; the problem is not about unnecessary calls but about reliable completion of the async
   update.

   D – Add executionContext.getEventArgs[].disableAsyncTimeout[]

   This method does not exist in the XRM SDK; attempting to use it would cause a runtime error and cannot
   influence the async timeout behavior.

   E – Add executionContext.getEventArgs[].preventDefault[]

   preventDefault is not a supported API for the OnSave event and would have no effect on the asynchronous
   update; it is unrelated to ensuring the related record is saved.

   Conclusion
   Enabling the AsyncO  nSave setting (B) and properly handling the asynchronous operation with a promise (C)
   together guarantee that the current record is saved and the related record is updated reliably and
   consistently. The other options either do not solve the timing problem or are not valid APIs.

1. OnLoad Event: TabStateChange events on tabs B and C

Why it is correct: Tab A is expanded by default, while tabs B and C are collapsed. Registering OnChange
events for fields located on collapsed tabs during the form's initial load causes an unnecessary performance
hit.

By shifting the script registration to the TabStateChange events of tabs B and C, the browser only loads and
binds those event handlers lazily—meaning the code executes only if and when a user explicitly clicks to
expand those specific tabs. This keeps the initial form loading time fast and responsive.

OnSave Event: OnChange events for the columns involved in the calculations

Why it is correct: Running synchronous, heavy calculation logic during a form's OnSave event is a major
architectural anti-pattern. It blocks the saving pipeline, increases form submission latency, and risks creating
dirty data fields or infinite loops.

Moving this calculation logic to the individual fields' OnChange events ensures that calculations run
immediately as soon as a user alters a dependent value. This provides real-time visual feedback to the user
and leaves the OnSave pipeline clean and lightweight.

questions.explanation:
Box 1: Webhook -
With Dataverse, you can send data about events that occur on the service to a web app by using webhooks. A
webhook is a lightweight HTTP pattern for connecting web APIs and services with a publish-and-subscribe
model. Webhook senders notify receivers about events by making requests to receiver endpoints with some
information about the events.
Webhooks enable developers and ISVs to integrate Dataverse data with their own custom code hosted on
external services.

Box 2: Azure Service Bus -
Service Bus provides a secure and reliable communication channel between Dataverse runtime data and
external, cloud-based line-of-business apps. This capability is especially useful in keeping disparate
Dataverse systems or other Dataverse servers synchronized with business data changes.

Box 3: Azure Event hub -
Azure Event Hubs is a big data streaming platform and event ingestion service. It can receive and process
millions of events per second. Data sent to an event hub can be transformed and stored by using any real-time
analytics provider or batching/storage adapters.
Note: The most popular approaches in Dataverse involve webhooks, Azure messaging (Service Bus, Event
Hubs), Azure Logic Apps, or Power Automate.

Correct Action: Configure entity relationships.
Explanation:
To enable BOMs (Bills of Materials) to include subcomponents, it is necessary to define relationships between
entities. In this case, the BOM entity would have a one-to-many (1:N) or many-to-many (N:N) relationship with
the Subcomponent entity (or itself if subcomponents are part of the same entity). Entity relationships are
essential for linking data, supporting hierarchical structures, and ensuring that subcomponents can be
logically associated with the parent BOM.

Entity relationships allow for deeper integration, such as cascading behaviors or related views.

​Requirement 2: Report who changed the BOM records and when the changes were made.
Correct Action: Configure entity auditing.
Explanation:
Entity auditing is designed to capture details about changes made to records, including which user made the
changes and when they were made. This feature provides a detailed audit history for records, which can be
used for reporting purposes to track modifications.
Why this is correct:
It provides historical data that includes timestamps and user information for all updates.
Change tracking, while useful for synchronization, does not provide this level of detail for reporting.

questions.explanation:
Box 1: IsOptimisticConcurrencyEnabled
On a multi-threaded and multi-user system like Power Apps, operations and data changes often happen in
parallel. A problem arises when two or more update or delete operations on the same piece of data happen at
the same time. This situation could potentially result in data loss. The optimistic concurrency feature provides
the ability for your applications to detect whether a table record has changed on the server in the time
between when your application retrieved the record and when it tries to update or delete that record.
Box 2: If-Match: Etag -
Use If-Match and If-None-Match headers with ETag values to check whether the current version of a resource
matches the one last retrieved, matches any previous version or matches no version. These comparisons form
the basis of conditional operation support. Dataverse provides ETags to support conditional retrievals,
optimistic concurrency, and limited upsert operations.

Background

Northwind Traders uses Microsoft Dynamics 365 Sales to manage its sales process. To better understand its
customers, Northwind Traders invests in a team of researchers who gather data from multiple sources. The
company stores the data it collects in a Microsoft Azure SQL Database. The company plans to use the data to
enrich account records and make the sales team more effective.

Environment

questions.explanation:
A. Basic authentication is the most suitable choice for configuring the authentication method for a custom
connector to the company's cloud-based ERP system.

Basic authentication allows for straightforward implementation, where the client sends a username and
password directly encoded in the HTTP headers. This method is particularly applicable for RESTful APIs,
which many cloud-based ERP systems use, providing a familiar mechanism to access the system’s features
securely. Furthermore, it does not require complex setup and is widely supported across various programming
environments.

Critique of Other Options:

B. Windows Active Directory authentication: This method is suited for scenarios requiring integration with
on-premises systems or environments heavily relying on Active Directory. However, it adds complexity in
cloud environments and is rarely supported for custom connectors outside enterprise applications, making it
less versatile than basic authentication in a cloud context.
C. Certificate-based authentication: Although this method offers high security by utilizing digital certificates,
it requires additional setup and management overhead, such as issuing and storing certificates. For many
cloud-based applications, this complexity can be excessive if basic authentication meets the security
requirements.
D. Passwordless authentication: While this method improves security by eliminating the need for passwords,
it is still relatively nascent and may lack the straightforward implementation needed for custom connectors.
Additionally, it often relies on multi-factor authentication frameworks that might not be fully compatible with
all ERP systems.

In summary, basic authentication strikes a balance between simplicity, compatibility, and sufficient security
for cloud-based ERP systems deployed through custom connectors.

AD is correct because it provides two effective methods to disable the synchronous plug-in during a data load
without affecting user operations.

Reasoning for Correct Answers:

        1. BypassCustomPluginExecution: By providing this optional parameter in the create request, the
            system can execute the creation of records without invoking the associated plug-ins. This allows the
            data load operation to proceed rapidly, as it circumvents the overhead introduced by the synchronous
            execution of plug-ins, which can cause performance bottlenecks.

       2. BypassPluginExecution property on the CrmServiceClient: Setting this property directly on the
            client instance ensures that all operations conducted via this client instance bypass plug-in
            execution. This method applies to all operations initiated by the client throughout the data load
            process, ensuring consistency and avoiding interaction with the synchronous plug-in for the entire
            duration.

Evaluation of Incorrect Options:

        1. SuppressCallbackRegistrationExpanderJob: This option is irrelevant as it does not address the need
            to bypass plug-in execution directly during record creation. Instead, it is related to asynchronous job
            processing and would not expedite data load without invoking the corresponding plug-ins.

       2. Disable the plug-in step prior to starting the data load: While technically feasible, this approach may
            introduce risks. Disabling a plug-in during operational hours could cause issues for other processes
            or users creating records concurrently, which contradicts the operational requirement not to affect
            user actions. It also necessitates additional steps for re-enabling the plug-in post-load, which adds
            administrative overhead and potential for errors.

In conclusion, options A and D provide structured, scalable solutions that conform to the requirements of the
scenario without risking simultaneous user operations.

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is A, basic authentication. Here's why:

When developing custom connectors for the Microsoft Power Platform to interact with external systems like a
cloud-based ERP, selecting the right authentication method is crucial. The goal is to securely and efficiently
allow Power Apps, Power Automate, and Power BI to access the ERP system's data and functionality.

Basic authentication involves sending a username and password with each request to the ERP system. While
not the most secure option, it is frequently the simplest to implement and is widely supported by various APIs
and web services, making it a common choice for initial integration, especially when other, more complex
options are not immediately viable or supported by the target ERP system.

Options B, C, and D are generally less suitable for custom connectors in the Power Platform context for
several reasons. Windows Active Directory authentication (B) is typically used within a Microsoft network
environment and relies on Kerberos or NTLM, which aren't typically exposed directly for cloud-to-cloud
integrations via custom connectors. Biometric authentication (C) and two-factor authentication (D), while more
secure, are designed for user-interactive scenarios. Custom connectors usually operate in the background,
requiring non-interactive authentication that is programmatically accessible. Implementing biometric or two-
factor would require significant overhead to handle authentication challenges, which often is not feasible with
current custom connector capabilities in Microsoft Power Platform.

Given the scenario emphasizes a simple and consumable authentication method, basic authentication
provides an easy-to-implement solution that aligns with the common capabilities supported in Power
Platform's custom connectors for backend ERP integrations. The simplicity makes it attractive as a starting
point or when the ERP's API only provides this less secure approach. Security should be improved as
subsequent phases allow.

For further research on custom connectors and authentication in Power Platform, consult the official
Microsoft documentation:

Create a custom connector from scratch
Authentication options in Power Platform Connectors

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is A: Add the Field Service tables to the solution. Here's why:

The error message indicating missing dependencies directly points to the core issue: the custom tables within
the solution rely on components (tables, columns, etc.) that exist within the Dynamics 365 Field Service
application. When the solution is imported into the test environment, the system checks for these
dependencies. If the Field Service application (and therefore its components) is not present in the test
environment, the import fails because the custom tables cannot find the lookup targets they are designed to
interact with.

Option B (Exporting the solution as unmanaged) does not address the root cause. Unmanaged solutions are
meant for development environments where customization and changes are frequently made. While exporting
as unmanaged might allow for more flexible modifications in the target environment, it doesn't magically
resolve missing dependencies. The dependencies are still missing, and the solution will likely still fail to
function correctly or import properly.

Option C (Adding the custom tables to the solution) is misleading because the custom tables are already in
the solution – that's where the problem originates. The issue isn't about including the custom tables, but
about including the things the custom tables depend on.

Option D (Install the Field Service application in test) is the most direct and effective approach. Installing the
Field Service application installs all the base tables, entities, workflows, and other components that the
custom tables reference through their lookup columns. Once Field Service is installed, the import of the
solution containing the custom tables should succeed because the dependencies will be resolved. The system
will find the Field Service tables and columns, allowing the lookup relationships to be established.

Cloud computing principles relevant here are dependency management and environment consistency. In
cloud environments, ensuring that all necessary components and dependencies are present in each
environment is critical for successful deployment and execution of applications. Reproducible environments
are essential for reliable testing and deployment practices. Failing to include dependencies will lead to errors
and application failures.

Therefore, the correct solution is to ensure the Field Service application, the source of the missing
dependencies, is present in the test environment by installing it.

questions.explanation:
The correct authentication method for a custom connector connecting to a cloud-based ERP system, as
stated, is D. Generic OAuth authentication. Here's why:

OAuth (Open Authorization) is a widely adopted, open standard protocol that enables secure delegated
access. It allows a user to grant a third-party application (in this case, the custom connector) limited access to
their resources on a service (the cloud-based ERP system) without sharing their credentials (username and
password). This aligns perfectly with modern cloud security best practices.

Let's analyze why the other options are less suitable:

A. Two-factor authentication (2FA): While 2FA enhances security, it's not an authentication method per se.
It's an additional layer on top of an existing method. 2FA typically relies on an underlying authentication
mechanism like username/password or OAuth. It doesn't provide the initial delegated access a connector
needs.

B. Windows Active Directory authentication: Active Directory is primarily used for managing users and
computers within an on-premises Windows domain. While Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) exists for cloud
environments, directly using Windows Active Directory authentication for a custom connector connecting to a
generic cloud-based ERP system would be cumbersome and might not be natively supported. Even if Azure
AD is in use, directly exposing user credentials for automated tasks is generally discouraged.

C. Biometric authentication: Biometric authentication (fingerprint, facial recognition, etc.) relies on physical
attributes and is generally suitable for direct user interaction, not for automated connectors that need to run
in the background without user intervention. It's impractical for a custom connector to authenticate using
biometric data.

Generic OAuth is the most flexible and secure choice because it can be easily configured within the custom
connector settings. The connector can request an access token from the ERP system’s authorization server
using the user's consent, and then use this token to access protected resources. The ERP system’s
authorization server will often support OAuth and allow the custom connector to be registered as a valid
client. This approach allows for granular control over the permissions granted to the connector, minimizing
security risks and adhering to the principle of least privilege. Furthermore, if the user's access rights change
in the ERP system, the access token can be revoked, immediately cutting off the connector's access.
Therefore, OAuth offers a secure, scalable, and manageable authentication mechanism ideally suited for
integrating custom connectors with cloud-based ERP systems.

Supporting links:

OAuth 2.0: https://oauth.net/2/
Microsoft Power Platform Connectors: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/connectors/custom-connectors/
Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) Authentication: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-
directory/develop/authentication-vs-authorization

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is B. IPluginExecutionContext.

Here's why:

The scenario describes a synchronous operation within Dataverse where a plugin needs to execute upon an
update to an Account record. The core requirement is to access the data related to that execution, specifically
the record being updated (including the old and new credit limit values).

IPluginExecutionContext is the fundamental interface that provides the context for plugin execution within
Dataverse. It offers access to essential data, including:

InputParameters: Values passed into the execution pipeline, such as the updated account record.
OutputParameters: Values being passed out of the execution pipeline.
PreEntityImages and PostEntityImages: Snapshots of the entity before and after the update, respectively,
which are crucial for comparing the old and new credit limits.

IServiceEndpointNotificationService is used for sending notifications asynchronously to external services,
not for retrieving data within a synchronous Dataverse operation.

IWebHttpServiceEndpointPlugin is a specialized interface for plugins that communicate with external web
services. While the overall solution involves Azure Service Bus, this interface isn't used for the initial trigger
and data access during the Dataverse update event. This interface would be used when sending the message
to Azure Service Bus after the plugin determines that the credit limit exceeds $25,000.

IServiceEndpointPlugin is a generic interface for creating service endpoints; it is not involved in triggering
plugins upon a data update or providing access to the execution context of that update.

Therefore, to access the pre- and post-update entity images and input parameters, the plugin must implement
IPluginExecutionContext. This interface provides the necessary tools to inspect the data changes and
determine if the credit limit has exceeded the specified threshold, triggering the subsequent logic for posting
to the Azure Service Bus. Without this, the plugin has no awareness of the changes happening in Dataverse.

Event Execution Pipeline in Microsoft Dataverse
IPluginExecutionContext Interface

questions.explanation:
UpsertRequest.
   The term "Upsert" is a combination of Update and Insert. The UpsertRequest message checks if a record
   already exists based on the primary key (GUID). If the record exists, it updates it. If it does not exist, it
   automatically creates a new record. This eliminates the need to perform a separate retrieval request first,
   minimizing API roundtrips.
   UpsertRequest
   External data systems rarely store Dataverse's system-generated GUIDs. Instead, they rely on business keys
   like an EmployeeID or SKU (custom columns). By targeting an Alternate key configured with these custom
   columns, UpsertRequest can determine whether a matching record exists in Dataverse. It then triggers either
   an update or a create operation exactly as it would with a primary key.
   Alternate key
   When you define an Alternate key on one or more custom fields, Dataverse builds a unique database index
   behind the scenes. This strictly ensures that no two records can share the exact same value combination for
   those columns. If a user or an integration tries to duplicate these values, Dataverse blocks the action and
   returns an error.

Scenario: User2 reports that Azure consumption for API calls has increased significantly to 100 calls per
   minute in the last month.
   Example:
   In the following example, the rate limit of 10 calls per 60 seconds is keyed by the caller IP address. After each
   policy execution, the remaining calls allowed in the time period are stored in the variable remainingCallsPerIP.
   <policies>
   <inbound>
   <base />
   <rate-limit-by-key calls="10"
   renewal-period="60"
   increment-condition="@(context.Response.StatusCode == 200)"
   counter-key="@(context.Request.IpAddress)"
   remaining-calls-variable-name="remainingCallsPerIP"/>
   </inbound>
   <outbound>
   <base />
   </outbound>
   </policies>
   Note: The rate-limit-by-key policy prevents API usage spikes on a per key basis by limiting the call rate to a
   specified number per a specified time period. The key can have an arbitrary string value and is typically
   provided using a policy expression. Optional increment condition can be added to specify which requests
   should be counted towards the limit. When this call rate is exceeded, the caller receives a 429 Too Many
   Requests response status code.
   Incorrect Answers:

questions.explanation:
You must replace ACTIONNAME in line AV22 with northwind_ValidateAddress: No.

In Dataverse, when executing a custom action from code, the Execute request typically uses the unique name
of the custom action. If the action is bound or unbound, the syntax might differ, but replacing a placeholder
with a hardcoded string directly into a line variable like that is generally not the correct way to handle Action
names in standard Dataverse SDK patterns.

You can add code at line AV28 to display an error message returned by the address validation API: Yes.

This is a valid practice. When calling an external API from a custom action, it is standard procedure to parse
the API response. If the response indicates a failure or validation error, you can catch that error and throw a
InvalidPluginExecutionException to display a meaningful message back to the user interface.

Calling the address validation API from the custom action eliminates the error reported by users: No.

Simply invoking an API does not inherently "eliminate" errors. If the API is called correctly but returns a
validation failure, the user will still see an error message. Furthermore, if the integration is not handled with
proper error boundaries (like try-catch blocks) or if the API endpoint is unavailable, the custom action itself
could fail, resulting in a system error rather than eliminating the user's issue.
